title: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The fine frilling of ammonite sutures is a surface-tension phenomenon

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The minutely branched, arborescent outline superposed on the lobes and saddles of some ammonite sutures, with branches ending in rounded arcs, is a surface-tension phenomenon of the same kind as the patterns made by milk on a greasy plate or oil on an alkaline solution.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Superposed upon the usual sinuous outline, with its “lobes” and “saddles,” we have here a minutely ramified, or arborescent outline, in which all the branches terminate in wavy, more or less circular arcs,—looking just like the ‘landscape marble’ from the Bristol Rhaetic. We have no difficulty in recognising in this a surface-tension phenomenon.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Septa of chambered shells”. Scope: ammonoids with complex (ammonitic) suture lines

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-21: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Suture morphology is abundant and measurable, but the analogical mechanism is weakly discriminating because reaction-diffusion, differential growth and buckling can produce similar branching. Existing data can test model fit, not confidently identify surface tension as the cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify branch topology, tip curvature and wavelength in ammonitic sutures and compare them with explicit surface-tension instability models and rival growth or buckling models. A surface-tension account must uniquely reproduce scaling and branching statistics, not merely visual resemblance.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Interfacial tensions during septum formation are not preserved.

Pattern resemblance is non-unique across physical mechanisms.

Many fossils expose only 2D suture traces.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.75
operationalizability: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.3
analysis feasibility: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Suture frills can be measured from open plates and scans, so the descriptive pattern is accessible for complex ammonitic sutures. Identifying that pattern as surface tension, by analogy with milk on a greasy plate or oil on alkali, does not specify a statistic that excludes buckling and other branching processes. Existing images can test the geometry and cannot isolate the physical cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify the fine branching of ammonitic sutures, including rounded terminal arcs, and compare those statistics with surface-tension fingering patterns and with buckling or wrinkling alternatives. A unique match to surface-tension geometry would support the claim; an equal or better match to another generator would leave it unresolved.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Rounded, arborescent outlines are produced by several interfacial instabilities, not only by surface tension.

Classical suture drawings emphasize the pattern the claim treats as diagnostic.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.5
data existence: 0.55
operationalizability: 0.5
discriminating power: 0.4
analysis feasibility: 0.55
